video.title: You Can Learn AI Agent Memory Layers | Graph RAG, Vector DB, SQLite, Hermes, Waku

protocol.status: second independent labeler (B), for the noise floor
protocol.note: Drafted from the transcript alone, without seeing any jevcut output.
protocol.times_from: Whisper small transcript; seconds in the source, so labels survive re-transcription

clips.why: How to maintain agent memory: add/delete/overwrite/no-op, or 'retire', which invalidates an old fact with a time range instead of deleting it (1,000 stars in 25 days, then 1.3k). The concrete example makes it land.
'Reflect' and dreaming: when the agent is idle, schedule a job to merge duplicates and drop stale memories, like a post-processing pass. It stands alone apart from a 'last but not least' opener.
Plain explanation of vector stores: words are embedded as high-dimensional numbers, found by similarity search (food near apple and sausages), and maintained by upsert/delete.

also_ok.why: Opener: LLM calls carry no long-term memory, so ChatGPT and Claude Code built memory systems; then the procedural/semantic/episodic pillars. A channel intro and the Waku pitch are mixed in.

How semantic memory gets built: log conversations to SQLite, consolidate every 5-10 turns with a cheap model, distill into memory.md; ends on 'memories are the most valuable asset of any agent harness'.

negatives.why: Repo plug (1.3k stars, pip install) that turns into an on-screen 'what's on my calendar' demo.
Funny moment (his Hermes agent talks like Pikachu, says 'Pikapi'), but it narrates a file on screen and makes no point.
Arena results read off the dashboard (4.6 s for SQLite, 7.5 s for LangMem, Zep still seeding): numbers with no standalone point.
Sounds like a verdict (graph memory may be overkill), but it's a reaction to the on-screen Zep graph ('this is doing its job').
Direct callout ('Zep team, please fix speed'): only makes sense after the demo.
